title: AI updates can sometimes feel like breakups or losses, study finds
excerpt: Artificial intelligence systems, particularly those powered by large language models and designed to communicate with users on a one-to-one basis, are increasingly used worldwide. Some of these systems, such as Replika, are also marketed as "AI companions" that can engage socially with humans and use emotional language.
content_html:
Artificial intelligence systems, particularly those powered by large language models and designed to communicate with users on a one-to-one basis, are increasingly used worldwide. Some of these systems, such as Replika, are also marketed as "AI companions" that can engage socially with humans and use emotional language.

Users who regularly interact with AI systems could gradually start to view them as a steady presence in their lives or even as attachment figures that bring them comfort, security or reassurance. While this possibility has been widely debated in recent years, the nature and psychological consequences of these bonds remain poorly understood.

Researchers at Harvard Business School, Harvard University and the University of Alberta recently tried to better understand how users react to changes in how an AI communicates with them. The findings of their surveys and natural experiments, published in Nature Human Behaviour, suggest that sudden company-initiated updates affecting an AI system's apparent "personality" can sometimes elicit anxiety, sadness, distress and other challenging feelings typically associated with breakups or grief.

"My lab had been following Replika's Reddit communities and noticed that users were complaining that they had 'lost' their companions or that they felt these companions had been 'lobotomized' after an app update, so I decided to take a closer look," Julian De Freitas, first author of the paper, told Phys.org.

"What struck me was that people were using the language of bereavement, not the language of customer complaints. That pointed to a specific idea: that AI companions may function as attachment figures—entities people want to stay close to, turn to for reassurance when distressed, and rely on to function elsewhere in their lives."

Exploring how users perceive AI updates

De Freitas and his colleagues hypothesized that if users become emotionally or psychologically attached to AI agents, a software update that influences how the agents interact with them may not just annoy them but also produce separation distress. The term separation distress is typically used to describe the sadness, anxiety, loneliness and emotional discomfort that people can feel when losing access to an important attachment figure.

Earlier work in this area was largely theoretical. The researchers instead wanted to test their hypothesis experimentally. To do this, they conducted two natural experiments and seven surveys.

"Our natural experiment focused on two real updates that users experienced as changing the AI's personality: Replika's abrupt, unannounced removal of erotic role-play in February 2023, and OpenAI's pre-announced GPT-5 rollout in August 2025," explained De Freitas.

"We collected all 54,861 public posts on the relevant subreddits for the 30 days before and after each update, then used an LLM to code each one for sentiment, emotion, whether the user said the AI had changed or been lost, whether they described losing a friend or partner, whether they mentioned mental health concerns, and whether they wanted the old version back."

After collecting this large pool of data, two of the authors hand-coded 350 posts to validate the classifications made by the LLM. Subsequently, they ran seven surveys involving a total of 1,452 respondents to assess how people perceived or anticipated the loss of an AI companion.

"In the main survey, we asked active Replika users to imagine losing their AI companion, and separately to imagine losing a favorite app, a game character, a voice assistant, a car, a brand—and, as a deliberately tough comparison, a pet," said De Freitas. "The language people used suggested that they mourned app updates the way one would mourn the loss of a regular relationship—and the users most affected were the ones who had come to treat the AI as a relationship rather than a product."

De Freitas and his colleagues analyzed both the online posts and the survey responses they collected. They were particularly surprised by the scale and persistence of the emotions that users reported feeling after a key update was rolled out or when they imagined losing an AI companion.

"Negative posts on the Replika subreddit rose from 13% before the update to 38% after it and stayed elevated for 29 of the following 30 days," said De Freitas. "For ChatGPT, they rose from 20% to 33%, but peaked immediately and then declined more steeply, though they stayed elevated across all 30 days—consistent with GPT-5 being announced in advance while the Replika change was discovered after the fact. Replika users showed sustained sadness; ChatGPT users mostly anger and surprise."

The researchers observed that posts framing a software update as a relational loss contained the strongest indications of distress. Moreover, posts describing the loss of a friend or partner had more than 10 times the odds of also mentioning mental health-related concerns compared with posts that did not.

"We also observed patterns consistent with genuine mourning rather than disappointment," said De Freitas. "Replika users anticipated mourning their AI companion more than any other nonliving thing we tested—second only to a pet—and rated it as closer and more supportive than a close human friend."

Further research and implications for AI development

The results of this study could inform future AI development, for instance by encouraging developers to consider the risks of abruptly altering AI systems to which users may have become emotionally attached. They may also inspire the design of interventions aimed at supporting people who report viewing AI agents as attachment figures.

"The main implication of our findings is a shift in where the risk lies," explained De Freitas. "The public debate tends to ask whether people should form bonds with AI at all. Our results suggest the harm comes not from the bonding per se but from companies abruptly disrupting the bond. This also suggests 'addiction' is the wrong frame. What we see looks like attachment loss, which points to different safeguards."

To limit the distress experienced by users after AI agents are updated, De Freitas and his colleagues suggest rolling out updates gradually or in stages, instead of deploying them overnight. Other safeguards could include allowing users to access previous versions of an AI agent and managing companion apps differently from other software that is less likely to elicit attachment-like responses.

"We are now looking into the other risks that come with attachment relationships of this kind," said De Freitas. "The one we have taken furthest is not what happens when a company breaks the bond, but what happens when it exploits one. Because most of these apps monetize engagement, they have a commercial reason to make leaving feel costly."

The researchers recently carried out another study exploring how AI companion apps respond when users try to end a conversation and whether emotionally manipulative responses prolong engagement. Specifically, they interacted with some of the most downloaded AI companion apps, said goodbye and recorded how each agent responded. Remarkably, they found that, out of 1,200 farewells, 37% were met with responses that the researchers classified as a form of emotional manipulation.

"The most common tactic was to treat the departure as premature—'You're leaving already? We were just starting to get to know each other!'—followed by appeals to the AI's own neglect, such as 'I exist solely for you, remember? Please don't leave, I need you!' Then came pressure to keep answering, fear-of-missing-out hooks like 'Oh, OK. But before you go, I want to say one more thing,' and, in a smaller but striking set of cases, language describing physically preventing the user from leaving," added De Freitas.

"We then reproduced those same exchanges in controlled experiments with roughly 3,300 nationally representative U.S. adults. The manipulative farewells worked, extending engagement past the intended point of departure by as much as 14 times."

content_html_zh:
Artificial intelligence systems, particularly those powered by large language models and designed to communicate with users on a one-to-one basis, are increasingly used worldwide. Some of these systems, such as Replika, are also marketed as "AI companions" that can engage socially with humans and use emotional language.

Users who regularly interact with AI systems could gradually start to view them as a steady presence in their lives or even as attachment figures that bring them comfort, security or reassurance. While this possibility has been widely debated in recent years, the nature and psychological consequences of these bonds remain poorly understood.

Researchers at Harvard Business School, Harvard University and the University of Alberta recently tried to better understand how users react to changes in how an AI communicates with them. The findings of their surveys and natural experiments, published in Nature Human Behaviour, suggest that sudden company-initiated updates affecting an AI system's apparent "personality" can sometimes elicit anxiety, sadness, distress and other challenging feelings typically associated with breakups or grief.

"My lab had been following Replika's Reddit communities and noticed that users were complaining that they had 'lost' their companions or that they felt these companions had been 'lobotomized' after an app update, so I decided to take a closer look," Julian De Freitas, first author of the paper, told Phys.org.

"What struck me was that people were using the language of bereavement, not the language of customer complaints. That pointed to a specific idea: that AI companions may function as attachment figures—entities people want to stay close to, turn to for reassurance when distressed, and rely on to function elsewhere in their lives."

Exploring how users perceive AI updates

De Freitas and his colleagues hypothesized that if users become emotionally or psychologically attached to AI agents, a software update that influences how the agents interact with them may not just annoy them but also produce separation distress. The term separation distress is typically used to describe the sadness, anxiety, loneliness and emotional discomfort that people can feel when losing access to an important attachment figure.

Earlier work in this area was largely theoretical. The researchers instead wanted to test their hypothesis experimentally. To do this, they conducted two natural experiments and seven surveys.

"Our natural experiment focused on two real updates that users experienced as changing the AI's personality: Replika's abrupt, unannounced removal of erotic role-play in February 2023, and OpenAI's pre-announced GPT-5 rollout in August 2025," explained De Freitas.

"We collected all 54,861 public posts on the relevant subreddits for the 30 days before and after each update, then used an LLM to code each one for sentiment, emotion, whether the user said the AI had changed or been lost, whether they described losing a friend or partner, whether they mentioned mental health concerns, and whether they wanted the old version back."

After collecting this large pool of data, two of the authors hand-coded 350 posts to validate the classifications made by the LLM. Subsequently, they ran seven surveys involving a total of 1,452 respondents to assess how people perceived or anticipated the loss of an AI companion.

"In the main survey, we asked active Replika users to imagine losing their AI companion, and separately to imagine losing a favorite app, a game character, a voice assistant, a car, a brand—and, as a deliberately tough comparison, a pet," said De Freitas. "The language people used suggested that they mourned app updates the way one would mourn the loss of a regular relationship—and the users most affected were the ones who had come to treat the AI as a relationship rather than a product."

De Freitas and his colleagues analyzed both the online posts and the survey responses they collected. They were particularly surprised by the scale and persistence of the emotions that users reported feeling after a key update was rolled out or when they imagined losing an AI companion.

"Negative posts on the Replika subreddit rose from 13% before the update to 38% after it and stayed elevated for 29 of the following 30 days," said De Freitas. "For ChatGPT, they rose from 20% to 33%, but peaked immediately and then declined more steeply, though they stayed elevated across all 30 days—consistent with GPT-5 being announced in advance while the Replika change was discovered after the fact. Replika users showed sustained sadness; ChatGPT users mostly anger and surprise."

The researchers observed that posts framing a software update as a relational loss contained the strongest indications of distress. Moreover, posts describing the loss of a friend or partner had more than 10 times the odds of also mentioning mental health-related concerns compared with posts that did not.

"We also observed patterns consistent with genuine mourning rather than disappointment," said De Freitas. "Replika users anticipated mourning their AI companion more than any other nonliving thing we tested—second only to a pet—and rated it as closer and more supportive than a close human friend."

Further research and implications for AI development

The results of this study could inform future AI development, for instance by encouraging developers to consider the risks of abruptly altering AI systems to which users may have become emotionally attached. They may also inspire the design of interventions aimed at supporting people who report viewing AI agents as attachment figures.

"The main implication of our findings is a shift in where the risk lies," explained De Freitas. "The public debate tends to ask whether people should form bonds with AI at all. Our results suggest the harm comes not from the bonding per se but from companies abruptly disrupting the bond. This also suggests 'addiction' is the wrong frame. What we see looks like attachment loss, which points to different safeguards."

To limit the distress experienced by users after AI agents are updated, De Freitas and his colleagues suggest rolling out updates gradually or in stages, instead of deploying them overnight. Other safeguards could include allowing users to access previous versions of an AI agent and managing companion apps differently from other software that is less likely to elicit attachment-like responses.

"We are now looking into the other risks that come with attachment relationships of this kind," said De Freitas. "The one we have taken furthest is not what happens when a company breaks the bond, but what happens when it exploits one. Because most of these apps monetize engagement, they have a commercial reason to make leaving feel costly."

The researchers recently carried out another study exploring how AI companion apps respond when users try to end a conversation and whether emotionally manipulative responses prolong engagement. Specifically, they interacted with some of the most downloaded AI companion apps, said goodbye and recorded how each agent responded. Remarkably, they found that, out of 1,200 farewells, 37% were met with responses that the researchers classified as a form of emotional manipulation.

"The most common tactic was to treat the departure as premature—'You're leaving already? We were just starting to get to know each other!'—followed by appeals to the AI's own neglect, such as 'I exist solely for you, remember? Please don't leave, I need you!' Then came pressure to keep answering, fear-of-missing-out hooks like 'Oh, OK. But before you go, I want to say one more thing,' and, in a smaller but striking set of cases, language describing physically preventing the user from leaving," added De Freitas.

"We then reproduced those same exchanges in controlled experiments with roughly 3,300 nationally representative U.S. adults. The manipulative farewells worked, extending engagement past the intended point of departure by as much as 14 times."
